articles.title: Extension Candidate: Amen Thompson
articles.excerpt: We explore Thompson's strengths and weaknesses and evaluate what a fair deal might look like for the Rockets guard.
articles.content:
This is the first installment in our 2026 series examining players who are prime candidates for rookie scale contract extensions. This series will explore the player’s strengths and weaknesses and evaluate what a fair deal between the player and his team might look like.

Background

The fourth overall pick in the 2023 draft after bypassing college in lieu of playing for the Overtime Elite league, Amen Thompson got off to a relatively slow start as a rookie in 2023/24, suffering an ankle injury in his fourth game and proceeding to miss 19 of his next 20 contests.

Through his first 30 appearances, the California native showed flashes of the special athleticism, talent and skills that made him a high lottery pick, averaging 6.8 points, 4.5 rebounds, 2.2 assists and 1.1 steals in just 16.7 minutes per game while shooting 48.8% from the field.

However, there was a major shift around the February 2024 trade deadline, as Thompson received far more playing time down the stretch as a rookie. He responded by averaging 12.1 PPG, 8.6 RPG, 3.0 APG, 1.4 SPG and 0.8 BPG in 27.6 MPG while shooting 56.3% from the floor across 32 outings.

The Rockets had won just 17, 20 and 22 games in the three seasons leading up to Thompson’s rookie campaign. But they went 41-41 in his first season, including a 30-32 mark when he was active.

Thompson built upon the second-half success he found as a rookie in year two, averaging 14.1 PPG, 8.2 RPG, 3.8 APG, 1.4 SPG and 1.3 BPG on 55.7% shooting in 69 games, including 42 starts (32.2 MPG). Notably, he finished fifth in Defensive Player of the Year voting and earned a spot on the All-Defensive first team.

Houston improved to 52-30 in 2024/25 and entered the playoffs as the No. 2 seed in the Western Conference. The team lost its first-round matchup against Golden State in seven games, with Thompson averaging 15.7 PPG, 6.9 RPG, 3.3 APG, 1.7 SPG and 0.9 BPG on 49.4% shooting in 33.1 MPG.

In the wake of a torn ACL to Fred VanVleet, Thompson was asked to initiate the offense far more often in 2025/26. He became a full-time starter as well, leading the NBA in total minutes (2,953; Kevin Durant was second at 2,840, while Jabari Smith Jr. was fifth with 2,705) and ranking second behind Tyrese Maxey (38.0) in minutes per game with 37.4.

Thompson averaged 18.3 PPG, 7.8 RPG, 5.3 APG, 1.5 SPG and 0.6 BPG on 53.4% shooting in 79 games last season. He played a critical role in the Rockets repeating repeating their 52-30 record, which was good for the fifth seed in the West and a first-round matchup against the Lakers. Houston lost that series in six games, with Thompson averaging 19.2 PPG, 7.0 RPG, 5.7 APG, 2.0 SPG and 1.2 BPG on 48.8% shooting in 44.0(!) MPG.

articles.title: Amen Thompson, Rockets Reportedly Agree to $208M Contract Extension, Updated Salary Cap
articles.excerpt: The Houston Rockets rewarded one of the NBA's rising young stars with a new deal on Thursday.
articles.content:
The Houston Rockets rewarded one of the NBA's rising young stars with a new deal on Thursday.

According to ESPN's Shams Charania, the Rockets and wing Amen Thompson agreed to a five-year, $208 million rookie-scale contract extension. The 2026-27 season was set to be the final year of Thompson's rookie deal with a salary of $12.3 million, so Thursday's extension is a major pay bump for the 23-year-old.

NBA Punishes Clippers

ESPN's Bobby Marks previously speculated that Thompson could receive a new deal "at or close to a five-year, $251 million extension." Keith Smith of Spotrac predicted that it would be a five-year, $185 million deal to match center Alperen Sengun. Marks pointed out that Thompson ranked 15th among 188 players by holding opponents to 42.8 percent shooting as the closest defender.

Kelly Iko of Yahoo Sports reported that Houston considers Thompson "the only near untouchable on the roster," and Thursday's deal signifies the team's commitment to him.

The Rockets also signed restricted free agent Tari Eason to a five-year, $81.5 million deal, keeping their core of young two-way wings intact.

After Houston selected Thompson with the No. 4 pick in the 2023 NBA draft, it didn't take him long to find his footing in the league. He followed up a solid rookie season with a strong sophomore campaign that resulted in an All-Defensive first team selection.

Thompson's third year in the NBA saw him grow even further while sharing the floor with star forward Kevin Durant. He averaged 18.3 points, 7.8 rebounds, 5.3 assists and 1.5 steals while starting 79 games. He led Houston with 37.4 minutes per game, and he remained the team's engine in the postseason, upping his average to 19.2 points in the first-round series against the Los Angeles Lakers as the Rockets were eliminated in six games.

Thompson has shown the potential to be a two-way star who can make an impact on both ends of the floor. Thursday's deal shows that Houston views him as a franchise cornerstone, and his role will continue to grow as the Rockets try to contend for an NBA title next season and beyond.

The Bills finished the season 12-5, losing in the divisional round to the Denver Broncos in overtime.

One of the most creative players, perhaps in league history, Allen is able to beat defenders over the top with deep shots while also finding receivers on short passes after plays break down.

At 6'5", 237 pounds, Allen can also run through and around defenders as well as any quarterback in the NFL today.

The 2024 MVP is sure to put together a strong campaign in 2026, but the biggest knock against Allen is his lack of postseason success. He and the Bills have yet to make it past the AFC Championship Game, often falling short to Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs.

Last year seemed like the best chance Allen has had to reach the Super Bowl since the Chiefs missed the playoffs, but Buffalo ultimately fell short to the Broncos.

A championship ring is the only thing keeping Allen from being in the same conversation with some of the all-time greats, and he'll look to get over the hump this year.

Garrett finished the 2025 campaign with 23 sacks, breaking the previous record of 22.5, held by Michael Strahan (2001) and T.J. Watt (2021). Garrett's previous career high for sacks was 16, so he reached a completely different level last season.

While Garrett was by far the most impactful defensive player in the NFL last season, it really didn't mean that much since he was on a lowly Cleveland Browns team that finished 5-12.

This year, it's a completely different story.

The Rams made the biggest move of the offseason when they acquired Garrett for linebacker Jared Verse and a haul of draft picks. Los Angeles already boasted one of the best offenses in the NFL, and bringing in Garrett quickly made the Rams the team to watch to win it all in 2026.

To make matters worse for opposing offenses, legendary defensive tackle Aaron Donald came out of retirement to join Garrett on the defensive line, meaning Los Angeles went from having a middling defense in 2025 to one of the best heading into this season.

articles.title: Dianna Russini's relationship with Mike Vrabel was 'clear violation,' The Athletic says
articles.excerpt: Dianna Russini's former company reviewed 903 stories, 204 podcasts and 77 videos as part of an internal review into her relationship with Patriots coach Mike Vrabel.
articles.content:
The Athletic has concluded its investigation into former NFL reporter Dianna Russini following her resignation in April on the heels of published photos of her and New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel.

Conducted by Mike Semel, an editorial director for standards and quality at The Athletic, the investigation ultimately concluded that Russini failed to disclose her conflict of interest regarding Vrabel. 

"Russini’s relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic’s standards," the report reads. "Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed."

Semel wrote that he reviewed 903 stories, 204 podcasts and 77 videos before releasing his report. He concluded "the vast majority of Russini’s work for The Athletic had nothing to do with Vrabel, the teams he was coaching or the players the team was pursuing." Semel added that most of Russini's coverage of Vrabel and the Patriots was "transactional and newsy." The review covered her journalistic work, not personal conduct, since she resigned from the company April 14, a week after Page Six first published photos of her and Vrabel holding hands at an Arizona resort.

"When first confronted with the photos by The New York Post, Russini waited two days before telling her editors and managers," Semel wrote. "She then told a story to explain the photos that did not align with facts, raising issues of trust."

About five percent of the stories written by Russini mentioned Vrabel, according to the report, but none included exclusive information that was not reported by other news organizations.

One story, a profile of Vrabel in 2024 during his year off from coaching between the Patriots and the Tennessee Titans written by another reporter, would not have happened were it not for the connection between Vrabel and Russini, who brokered a meeting with Vrabel that led to the story. Semel found no inaccuracies in any of Russini's story about Vrabel or his teams.

The photographs of Russini and Vrabel "indicate a relationship that puts The Athletic’s credibility in jeopardy and gives the appearance of a conflict of interest," Semel wrote.

The investigation also included interviews with 14 Athletic staffers who worked most closely with Russini.

A New York Times story from June reported Russini no longer considers herself a journalist.

articles.title: The Athletic’s review of Dianna Russini’s work concludes she was ‘noncompliant’ with standards
articles.excerpt: The NFL insider resigned in April after photos with her and New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel were published.
articles.content:
Dianna Russini in Feb. 2022. Jeff Kravitz / FilmMagic

Ex-NFL insider Dianna Russini violated The Athletic’s standards because of her undisclosed relationship with New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel, a lengthy inquiry conducted by the publication concluded.

“Specifically, when it comes to The Athletic’s standards, Russini was noncompliant,” the report said.

The inquiry, which was publicly released Thursday, drew no conclusions about the full extent of the Russini-Vrabel relationship, which has been the subject of speculation after a media firestorm this spring. It also found scant evidence that it impacted Russini’s or The Athletic’s reporting on Vrabel and his teams.

Russini resigned from The Athletic in April following pictures published by the New York Post’s Page Six that showed Russini and Vrabel together at a Sedona, Ariz., resort. The two were the only ones in the photos in which they were captured appearing to hold hands, hug, and, in one instance, sit in a pool together. The whole episode, from the pictures being published to her resignation, took place over one week.

“We neither completed an investigation nor reached any conclusion about the nature of the full relationship between Vrabel and Russini, but the totality of the public photographs are enough to conclude a violation of company policy,” the report said.

Before the Page Six photos, Russini, 43, was considered a star reporter, dueling with the top NFL insiders for scoops during her nearly three years at The Athletic. She joined the platform after eight years at ESPN.

When reached for comment on the report, Russini declined to be interviewed, but gave a statement saying, “I stand by any and all reporting I’ve ever done in my career.”

A spokesperson for The Athletic declined further comment.

Mike Semel, The Athletic’s editorial director for standards and editorial quality, conducted the full review of Russini’s work regarding Vrabel.

In the inquiry, which lasted nearly five months since the announcement of an investigation, Semel wrote that he viewed 903 stories and 77 videos published on The Athletic’s site that Russini either authored or contributed to. Semel watched or listened to 204 of Russini’s “Scoop City” podcasts for The Athletic and 25 off-platform appearances in which Russini represented the company. He also studied 75 stories by The Athletic of events involving Vrabel and his teams and compared them to coverage in other publications.

Semel said he interviewed “approximately 14” Athletic staffers, who had worked with Russini. Russini was not asked to participate in the review of her work, according to a source briefed on the process who was not authorized to speak publicly about the report.

While the full nature of the Russini-Vrabel relationship is still unknown, the vast majority of Russini’s work for The Athletic had nothing to do with Vrabel, the report said. Of the 903 pieces, around 5 percent were in some way about Vrabel or his teams. Of the around 46 pieces that mentioned Vrabel or his teams, nearly a third were transactional moves about trades or hires. None of them were scoops, meaning The Athletic did not report the stories exclusively.

Semel said he did not investigate Russini’s personal conduct because she was no longer an employee of the company, but he continued to examine her journalism.

“Russini should have disclosed to The Athletic the nature of her relationship with Vrabel to allow editors to assess the kinds of stories on which she should have been working, if any,” Semel concluded. “She did not.”

While the inquiry reached no conclusion on whether the Russini-Vrabel relationship was romantic, Semel noted that Russini, after Page Six confronted her about the photos in April, waited two days before telling her editors and managers.

The Athletic’s executive editor Steven Ginsberg initially supported Russini in a statement as she denied there was anything untoward.

“The photos don’t represent the group of six people who were hanging out during the day,” Russini said in a statement upon the publication of the Page Six story in April.

As more information came in, The Athletic, which is owned by The New York Times, adjusted its stance. Shortly after, Russini was suspended from reporting for The Athletic. She resigned a week after the Page Six story was published.

In regards to the initial reaction, the inquiry found that Russini “told a story to explain the photos that did not align with the facts, raising issues of trust.”

Although Russini’s conduct was deemed not up to standards, the report found limited evidence that she favored Vrabel in her writings or analysis.

“Most of what Russini wrote about Vrabel or the Patriots was transactional and newsy,” Semel wrote. “In addition, I’ve not found a clear link to conclude that Russini used her platform to promote Vrabel or help his teams during her time at The Athletic.”

Semel did note that there were a few times Russini wrote glowingly about Vrabel “that in hindsight are awkward or even uncomfortable.”

In a column last October, she said that Vrabel returned to face his former team, the Tennessee Titans, as “New England’s hero.” Semel did not find Russini’s tone for the struggling Titans and the resurgent Patriots much different than other outlets’ coverage. She was also effusive about Vrabel on a few occasions on her “Scoop City” podcast, Semel said.

During her nearly three years with the platform, The Athletic published three in-depth stories on Vrabel, Semel said. Russini only had a byline on one of them, contributed to gaining access for another reporter on another, and had nothing to do with a third.

For an inside story about Vrabel’s gap year between his Titans and Patriots head coaching jobs by reporter Zack Rosenblatt in January 2025, Semel concluded it “likely would not have happened” without Russini’s involvement. Rosenblatt came up with the idea and asked Russini to set up a meeting with Vrabel. Russini arranged it but had nothing to do with the story that Rosenblatt had a solo byline on, according to Semel.

Russini also co-bylined an analysis with Joe Rexrode in January 2024. Rexrode, the inquiry said, obtained the key information for the story. Semel said that Russini should have disclosed her relationship with Vrabel for the piece, though it “was straight down the middle and fact-based.”

In December 2023, in Russini’s “What I’m hearing” column, there was an item buried deep inside about the reasoning behind Vrabel’s Titans going for a sabermetric-based two-point conversion.

In all, Semel recommended an “Editor’s Note” be placed on this column and on three videos.

“Of the 77 videos that featured Russini, three were specific to Vrabel,” Semel wrote. “Two were done at a joint preseason practice between the Vikings and Patriots in August 2025. They were light-hearted (“50 seconds of questions for Vrabel’s 50th birthday” and “What annoys Mike Vrabel?”).

(She similarly did quick takes with Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell at the same event.)

“The third was also somewhat light-hearted about a training camp fight between the Patriots and Commanders. In it, Russini discusses Vrabel’s role in breaking up the fight, and he comes across as somewhat heroic. Summary

Seoul police referred Bang Si-hyuk, chairman of HYBE, to prosecutors Thursday over allegations that he lied to early investors before the company’s listing. He is accused of unfair trading under the Capital Markets Act, and police did not seek an arrest warrant. Financial authorities put his alleged improper gains at nearly 200 billion won, while Bang has denied wrongdoing. Prosecutors are expected to review the police file before deciding on indictment.

Key Facts

  • Police alleged that in 2019 Bang told existing shareholders that the company had no plans for an initial public offering while BigHit was already moving through preliminary listing procedures.
  • The shares were sold to a special purpose company set up by a private equity fund tied to Bang, and the fund sold them after the company listed in 2020.
  • The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency’s financial crime investigation unit opened the case in December 2024 and raided HYBE’s Yongsan headquarters in July of last year.
  • Published Sep 3, 2026 1:29 pm KST
  • Updated Sep 3, 2026 2:12 pm KST

HYBE Chairman Bang Si-hyuk appears at the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency's financial crime investigation unit in Mapo District, Seoul, Sept. 15, 2025, for questioning over alleged violations of the Capital Markets Act's ban on unfair trading. Korea Times file

Seoul police referred Bang Si-hyuk, chairman of HYBE, the entertainment giant behind boy band BTS, to prosecutors Thursday over allegations that he deceived early investors in the agency into selling their stakes before the company went public.

Police did not request an arrest warrant for him.

Bang is accused of unfair trading in violation of the Capital Markets Act. The police alleged that in 2019, when HYBE was still known as BigHit Music, he told existing shareholders that the company had no plans for an initial public offering, prompting them to sell their shares to a special purpose company set up by a private equity fund tied to him, even as BigHit was already moving through preliminary listing procedures.

The fund sold the shares after the company listed in 2020, and police believe Bang collected roughly 30 percent of the proceeds under an undisclosed agreement. Financial authorities have put his improper gains at nearly 200 billion won ($145 million).

The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency's financial crime investigation unit opened the case in December 2024 and raided HYBE's Yongsan headquarters in July of last year. Prosecutors turned back arrest warrant requests from police in April and May, demanding a supplementary investigation each time and prolonging the probe.

Bang has denied wrongdoing and has maintained that the listing was carried out in compliance with the relevant laws and regulations. Prosecutors are expected to review the police file before deciding whether to indict him.

Bang founded BigHit in 2005 and BTS debuted in 2013. The group's global breakthrough turned the label into the country's largest music company. Bang later stepped back from day-to-day management to chair HYBE's board and remains its single largest shareholder.

articles.title: What the Chiefs see in rookie Cyrus Allen — and the obstacle that remains
articles.excerpt: Here's the backstory of how Allen landed with the Chiefs in the fifth round of the 2026 NFL Draft.
articles.content:
NFL Preseason

Cyrus Allen has been one of the Chiefs' stars of the summer, but rookie wide receivers typically need time to get fully comfortable with Andy Reid's playbook. Jay Biggerstaff / Imagn Images

Kansas City Chiefs coach Andy Reid is ready to tell a training camp story.

It’s two weeks ago in his office dorm room at Missouri Western, and in a short anecdote, Reid is about to reveal exactly where the Chiefs stand when it comes to the potential of fifth-round receiver Cyrus Allen.

While also speaking about some of the expected pitfalls the rookie could face.

Reid said it was evident then that Allen was still getting all the play calls down. During practices — and also the first preseason game against the Los Angeles Rams — he wasn’t always ending up where he was supposed to.

What happened immediately after, though, Reid says, is just important.

“Even when there were a couple routes he ran the wrong thing and lined up the wrong way in the game, the quarterback still threw the ball to him. He made the catch,” Reid said with a smile. “You go, ‘All right. There’s a certain trust there.’ And he’ll work through all the other stuff.”

This is where the complexity lies with Allen — and also in trying to predict his rookie season, even after he was one of the team’s top performers during August’s practices.

The flashes have been there. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes labeled Allen as one of the team’s standouts at the end of training camp, and the fact that he kept peppering him with the ball while covered in the summer’s organized team activities signaled that the young receiver has already built up chemistry with his QB.

There’s a reason, though, that rookie receivers typically need time to become fully comfortable with Reid’s extensive playbook.

After the team’s second preseason game against Tampa Bay, Allen acknowledged in the locker room that recalling information remains an obstacle as he trains at all three receiver positions.

“Just slowing down my thought process,” Allen said when describing what he was working on most, “and just having to learn everything.”

Zoom out to the bigger picture — while projecting not just this season but the next four — and it’s easy to see why the Chiefs have been so encouraged by Allen.

Reid is quick to say he’s “got tools in there that work in this offense.” Receiver teammate Xavier Worthy has called Allen an “electric route runner,” while assistant general manager Mike Bradway says he takes coaching well with a unique skill set.

“We try to temper expectations a little bit, but you can just be out here watching him move around,” Bradway told The Athletic at training camp on Aug. 19. “You can tell he belongs.”

Allen’s path to Kansas City — and the NFL — wasn’t always direct. He wasn’t invited to the NFL combine, which meant teams had to do extra work to figure out if he was worth adding as a late-round draft pick.

Through it all, Allen said the Chiefs remained one of the most interested teams in him from the start.

It meant something a few months ago — and still does now.

“I appreciate that, for them having me here,” Allen said. “So I’ve got to make them right.”

Getting a head start

Immediately after his pro day at Cincinnati in late March, Allen was on the road to Kansas City.

The Chiefs scheduled him for his first top-30 visit. And Allen said the timing wasn’t a coincidence.

“They were honest with me,” Allen said. “They were like, ‘You’re a dawg. We wanted you here. That’s why we got you up here early.'”

Chiefs vice president of player personnel Ryne Nutt said in April that Allen’s impressive run through the all-star game circuit demanded the team take an extended look.

Allen first stood out at the American Bowl, with Nutt saying he was “routing up dudes left and right” while displaying quickness and elite route-running ability. After that, Allen was just as impressive against better competition in the Senior Bowl, which moved him further up the Chiefs’ board.

“Throughout the process,” Nutt said, “we just felt like he crushed it.”

That continued during Allen’s top-30 visit in K.C.

Bradway remembered talking with Allen in his office for about 15 minutes, with his demeanor standing out immediately.

“The kid was just a ton of juice, ton of confidence, ton of personality,” Bradway said. “He carries himself like he knows he’s a good player, and he’s used that slight at the combine for motivation.”

A recent comparison

Chiefs northeast area scout Cassidy Kaminski, meanwhile, said in April that his chat with Allen stood out as “one of the best interviews that I had.” Allen’s tone reflected some New Orleans swagger from his hometown, yet his words also came across as both passionate and authentic.

In terms of competitive energy and bravado, Kaminski immediately flashed back to his first interactions with former Chiefs running back Isiah Pacheco — a hard-nosed player who helped set the practice tone during his four seasons with the team.

Kaminski also said Allen’s coaches at Cincinnati gave positive reviews about how he bounced back from a dislocated elbow before his senior season. Allen’s work ethic then seemed to reflect a bigger theme about who he was.

“Yeah, he’s 185 pounds,” Kaminski said, “but pound-for-pound, you’re not going to question this kid’s toughness in any capacity.”

The Chiefs had all this in mind before reshuffling their NFL Draft board on Day 3.

Bradway said a pair of skill-position players, Allen and Nebraska running back Emmett Johnson, moved toward the top of the team’s list based on their on-field traits and willingness to take coaching. Those two also had consensus buy-in across the organization among coaches, scouts and support staff, who all believed that they’d be productive with the Chiefs.

K.C. traded up to select Johnson with the 161st pick, then took Allen after that at No. 176.

Almost immediately, Bradway said he heard from colleagues outside the building about Allen.

“He’s one of those guys where you pick him, and you get a ton of texts from guys around the league saying, ‘We really liked him,'” Bradway said. “It was one of those where the process kind of pays off — where you really identify a guy months before the draft.”

What’s next for Allen

While it’s too early to know how all this will end up, Allen has certainly made good on his first impression.

As early as June, Worthy was saying Allen had a “special ability to him.” Bradway also says some of the Chiefs’ scouting beliefs about Allen were reinforced during his first few months; most notably, Allen plays faster on the field than his 4.47-second 40-yard dash time would suggest, and he also shows an innate feel for how to get open against man coverage.

The Chiefs’ internal feelings about Allen also have been reflected in the moves they didn’t make. While many outsiders suggested they should add a veteran receiver as insurance, the fact they didn’t shows that they’ve seen enough from Allen not to want to block some of his expected playing time with another body.

Now, of course, comes the hard part — even if it might sound simple to most of the outside world.

Receivers coach Chad O’Shea says the biggest hurdle for Allen is getting accustomed to NFL play calls. That means getting in the huddle, processing the quarterback’s words, getting lined up correctly to the left or right side of the formation, then positioning with the exact alignment and split to ensure proper spacing with teammates.

“All those things are new, and they’re new to most players who are rookies in this league,” O’Shea said on Aug. 19. “We’ve just got to continue to really focus on those things, and great things will happen if we focus on the little things.”

It’s that hidden part of the game that has kept rookie receivers from getting early production in Reid’s offense before. And that’s not even taking into account that Allen is working to learn all of the Chiefs’ receiver positions — something the team doesn’t typically ask of its wideouts early in their rookie years.

The good news, for now? Reid has seen someone in Allen who isn’t afraid to challenge himself.

“We’ve loaded him up, and we’ve moved him around, which is tough,” Reid said. “But that’s what he wants. He wants to learn it all. But the more he plays, the better.”

Allen says he’s taking all the feedback seriously. Following the team’s second preseason game, he said one of his top accomplishments was correcting alignment issues Reid had brought up in previous days.

It’s the type of growth that’s made Allen confident in his abilities over time.

While giving the Chiefs hope that his best football is ahead.

“I put myself in this shell to where I’m just going to outwork you,” Allen said. “And it’s gonna show on the field.”

Tropical Depression Edouard is unleashing heavy rain and flash flooding in Texas and Louisiana, and will continue to do so through Wednesday, after making landfall Tuesday afternoon.

The tropical depression made landfall near Johnson Bayou, Louisiana, roughly 15 miles south-southeast of Port Arthur, Texas, at 3:20 p.m. EDT, packing maximum sustained winds of 60 mph and a minimum central pressure of 996 mb, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).

Edouard reached land while maintaining tropical storm status before weakening to a tropical depression Tuesday night.

The National Weather Service warned that low-lying and urban areas are particularly vulnerable to flash floods. The NWS also said river flooding might be possible along Edouard's track.

Edouard is expected to be post-tropical or simply remnants by Wednesday morning, but the rain will still linger into the evening hours as the circulation holds up, the FOX Forecast Center said.

Edouard is a small storm in terms of overall size, with tropical-storm-force winds extending just up to 25 miles from its center, meaning the heaviest pockets of rain will likely be more localized.

articles.title: MrBeast Teams Up With Google Gemini, Health
articles.excerpt: MrBeast signs multi-year deal with Google to feature Gemini AI, Google Health
articles.content:
YouTube's biggest creator just landed one of the tech industry's biggest brand deals. Jimmy Donaldson, the man behind MrBeast, is entering a multi-year partnership with Google that'll weave Gemini and Google Health into his content empire, according to a Google Keyword Blog announcement. It's a bet that pairs the internet's most-watched creator with Google's push to make AI feel less like software and more like a sidekick for everyday life.

Google just found itself a new spokesperson, and he's not your typical brand ambassador. The company announced a multi-year partnership with Jimmy Donaldson, better known to the internet as MrBeast, that'll bring Gemini and Google Health into his massively popular video format. The announcement came from Marvin Chow, Google's VP of Consumer and AI Marketing, who framed the deal as a way to turn 'impossibly big ideas into reality,' a phrase that could double as MrBeast's entire career pitch.

If you've been anywhere near YouTube in the last few years, you know what MrBeast content looks like: giant stunts, giant giveaways, giant production budgets. Donaldson built an audience north of 300 million subscribers by making everything bigger than it needs to be, and now Google wants a piece of that scale for its AI assistant. Pairing Gemini with a creator whose entire brand is built on spectacle is a pretty clear signal that Google isn't just trying to win over developers and enterprise customers anymore. It wants Gemini baked into pop culture.

The Google Health angle is the more interesting wrinkle here. Google has spent years trying to get its health and fitness tools, think Fitbit integrations and wellness tracking, into the daily habits of regular people, with mixed results against competitors like Apple and its tightly integrated Health app ecosystem. Bringing in a creator with MrBeast's reach could be Google's attempt to make health tech feel less clinical and more like something worth paying attention to, especially for a younger audience that watches Donaldson's videos religiously but might never open a health app on their own.

Advertisement

This isn't Google's first attempt to make Gemini feel culturally relevant. The company has leaned hard into consumer marketing for its AI products over the past year, competing directly with OpenAI's ChatGPT for mindshare among everyday users, not just power users and developers. Landing a creator of MrBeast's magnitude is arguably a bigger swing than a Super Bowl ad, given that his videos routinely pull in tens of millions of views within days of posting, often outperforming traditional broadcast audiences.

Industry watchers will be paying close attention to execution here. Celebrity and creator tie-ins with AI products have had a rocky history. Plenty of brand partnerships end up feeling bolted-on, more advertisement than genuine integration. The test for Google will be whether Gemini shows up in MrBeast's videos as something people actually use and talk about, versus a product placement viewers scroll past. Given that Donaldson has built his reputation on hyper-transparent, almost documentary-style content about how his stunts get made, there's a real opportunity for Gemini to be shown solving actual problems on camera rather than just getting name-dropped.

There's also a competitive subtext worth noting. Meta, Amazon, and other tech giants have all chased creator partnerships to varying degrees, but few have paired a single creator with both an AI assistant and a health platform simultaneously. That dual-pronged approach suggests Google sees this less as a one-off marketing stunt and more as a long-term platform play, using Donaldson's audience as a testing ground for how AI and health tools get adopted by a generation that grew up on YouTube rather than cable television.

Advertisement

What happens next will say a lot about where this goes. If early content performs well, expect Google to expand the partnership into more structured campaigns, possibly tying Gemini features directly into MrBeast's challenge videos or using Google Health data as a plot device in fitness-themed content. If it flops, it joins a long list of tech-meets-influencer collaborations that generated headlines but little lasting impact. Either way, the deal marks one of the most high-profile attempts yet to make an AI assistant feel like a character in someone's story rather than a tool buried in a search bar.

For everyday readers, this partnership is a preview of where AI marketing is headed: less about feature lists and more about embedding assistants into the content people already watch obsessively. Whether Gemini becomes a genuine part of MrBeast's storytelling or just a logo in the corner of the screen will determine if this is a landmark AI-creator deal or another forgettable brand tie-in. Either way, expect more tech giants to chase similar creator partnerships as the race for AI mindshare shifts from search bars to YouTube thumbnails.

articles.excerpt: It took much longer than expected.
articles.content:
It took much longer than expected. In the end, it didn’t say much (if anything) that was unexpected.

The Athletic has posted its internal review of former NFL Insider Dianna Russini’s reporting, following her resignation in the wake of the revelation of her relationship with Patriots coach Mike Vrabel.

“Russini’s relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic’s standards,” writes Mike Semel, who conducted the probe. “Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed.”

Semel cites the standard The Athletic believes Russini violated: “When reporting and writing stories we do not have an agenda and it is important that our readers understand that. If our readers question our adherence to that basic tenet of journalism, our credibility will be at stake. To maintain the highest form of authority we should avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest and reveal those sources or affiliations that may put into question our ability to be credible.”

Complicating the problem for Russini was the company’s conclusion that she did not handle the situation in an ideal manner, once the first images of Russini with Vrabel at a resort in Arizona were published.

"[W]hen first confronted with the photos by The New York Post,” Semel explains, “Russini waited two days before telling her editors and managers. She then told a story to explain the photos that did not align with facts, raising issues of trust.”

Semel nevertheless found few irregularities or issues that will require the attachment of an editor’s note: (1) a video regarding a 2025 training-camp fight in which Vrabel “comes out as somewhat heroic” for his role in breaking it up; and (2) a blurb in a column regarding the Titans’ decision to go for two in a specific game.

As to the accuracy of her reporting on matters involving Vrabel, Semel cited this quote from Russini in 2023, before the Titans fired Vrabel: “Angry Tennessee Titans fans can stop hoping owner Amy Adams Strunk fires Vrabel. It’s not happening. Based on multiple conversations with high-ranking Titans officials, the franchise strongly and collectively believes it has the right coach for long-term success.”

The report apparently concludes all matters between The Athletic and Russini. And it likewise concludes the story — unless and until Russini tells her version of it.

If she hopes to make the biggest splash and cause the most potential chaos, Tuesday, September 8 (the night before the Patriots-Seahawks regular-season opener), continues to be the ideal date for her next move.

articles.title: Final Fantasy 7 Remake Finale's Long-Awaited Release Date Officially Confirmed
articles.excerpt: Ssquare Enix announced during today's State of Play that Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will conclude the trilogy in April
articles.content:
The remake trilogy concludes in April 2027

Square Enix has finally announced a release date for Final Fantasy 7 Revelation. The finale to the remake trilogy based on the original 1997 RPG will be released on April 8, 2027. But that's not all that Square Enix had to reveal about the final chapter in the Final Fantasy 7 remake project.

Director Naoki Hamaguchi appeared during today's State of Play to announce the release date with a new trailer. Square Enix also shared over ten minutes of gameplay. Combat received significant, showing off the new FITS system that allows characters to use abilities tied to outfits. It is sort of like how Final Fantasy X-2 and Lightning Returns tie traditional jobs to different outfits. The Highwind airship will be the gang's base of operations and can be customized throughout the game. A silly addition to Revelation is the ability to fast-forward through cutscenes. It is meant to let players enjoy the game at their own pace, but watching a cutscene at 2x speed was almost incomprehensible.

You'll also be able to switch between party members at will in the open world. That will have an impact on how you approach quests. Small story beats and interactions with characters in the world will change depending on which party member you put in the lead. Some characters will have their own special quest lines as well. Fans of the card game Queen's Blood will want to pursue the new saga starring Red XIII.

What we know about Final Fantasy 7 Revelation

Square Enix revealed the finale to the remake trilogy during Summer Game Fest earlier this year, announcing it would be titled Revelation. The reveal trailer offered a brief look at the game's new systems and characters. Revelation will introduce the complete party, including Vincent Valentine and Cid Highwind. Players will also pilot the Highwind airship around Revelation's open world. While the finale will introduce new locations on top of returning areas from Remake and Rebirth, Hamaguchi has assured fans that it won't have the same level of content bloat as the second game in the trilogy. A trailer shown during Gamescom Opening Night Live gave a look at the Weapons, superbosses that will offer some of the most challenging fights in the game.

As for how Revelation will handle the trilogy's conclusion, Hamaguchi has said the development team isn't changing their plans based on player feedback. The director has said the team has had a clear vision for the series since the beginning, and that hasn't changed. But exactly what that plan is remains unclear. The remake trilogy's first two entries have played around with events from the original game, so players are still unsure if Cloud and the rest of the party will be able to change their fates.

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will be released on April 8, 2027 for Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X.

WASHINGTON (AP) — Billionaire investor Leon Black refused to appear for a sworn deposition before Congress on Thursday and instead sued the House Oversight Committee, asking a federal court to block subpoenas issued as part of its investigation into disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

The House Oversight Committee served Black with two subpoenas during a closed-door voluntary interview in June after lawmakers said he refused to answer questions about nondisclosure agreements. Black is the co-founder and former chief executive of the private equity firm Apollo Global Management. He stepped down in 2021 during the fallout over his ties to Epstein.

He is among a number of influential figures to appear in the investigation into Epstein and the web of wealth and influence around him. articles.title: Nvidia’s Hugging Face Acquisition Is a $12.9 Billion Bet on Open-Source AI
articles.excerpt: The long-rumored deal will give the chip giant access to—and help it promote—a huge repository of open-source AI models and data sets.
articles.content:
Nvidia has agreed to acquire Hugging Face, which makes online developer tools and maintains a massive library of open-source data sets, for nearly $13 billion. While the deal had been rumored for weeks, the companies made it official Thursday morning.

The deal signals Nvidia’s seriousness about being steeped in the software side of generative AI development as well as in infrastructure. Nvidia already offers customers a suite of free, customizable open-weights AI models, known as Nemotron. As part of its announcement, Nvidia committed to maintaining Hugging Face’s current open standards, suggesting that the chipmaker is positioning itself as an even greater resource for developers looking to access cutting-edge, nonproprietary tools.

The move also underscores Nvidia’s position that open-weights models are better for the tech industry than closed, proprietary AI models like those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic. Earlier this month, Nvidia rallied more than 80 companies to sign an open letter asking the US government to defend open-weight AI models. Nvidia also launched an initiative called SAFE, or Shared AI Findings Exchange, that encouraged tech companies to “confidentially collect and analyze AI incidents and near misses, identify recurring control failures and publish evidence-based operating recommendations that reduce systemic risk.”

“Open models let startups, businesses, universities and public institutions build on advanced capabilities without training every model from scratch,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in the press release announcing the deal. “AI advances faster when people can build together.”

Nvidia’s embrace of open-source software and open-weights AI might seem like an abrupt turn, especially given that CUDA, the software layer for its highly coveted GPUs, is itself proprietary. But as frontier AI labs and some of the large hyperscalers, including Amazon and Meta, seek to build their own custom chips, Nvidia has begun to position itself as a maker of not just GPUs but also high-performance CPUs, and has widened its software offerings in order to keep developers building on Nvidia’s platforms.

Business Insider previously reported that the two companies were in talks, and The Information later reported that a deal had been reached.

Hugging Face was founded a decade ago by three French entrepreneurs in New York City, who wanted to launch an AI “companion” app. That didn’t catch on, but the team’s efforts to build their own natural language processing (NLP) tools inspired their next move: making complex tech tools more accessible to developers. Hugging Face eventually became a platform for developers to freely share source code, data sets, and, in the generative AI era, large language models.

“Open-source AI is at an inflection point,” wrote Hugging Face cofounder and CEO Clément Delangue in a post on X announcing the acquisition. “Thanks to the community, we’ve shown that it can be a complement, and even an alternative, to closed-source APIs. But for it to happen at larger scale, it needs more compute, more support, more collaboration and more visibility.”

According to PitchBook data, Hugging Face had raised nearly $400 million in venture capital funding as of December 2025. Some of its backers include Betaworks, Lux Capital, Sequoia Ventures, Coatue, and Addition. Notable individual investors include Greg Brockman, Richard Socher, and the NBA player Kevin Durant.

Hugging Face has more recently been front and center after its platform was hacked by AI agents from OpenAI. The incident sparked a broader conversation across the tech industry about the safety, security, and manageability of the autonomous agents being touted by top AI companies.

In a 2023 interview with CNBC Delangue predicted that the number of developers working with AI models would soar, and estimated that within five years, “you’re going to have like 100 million AI builders. And if all of them use Hugging Face all day, every day, we’ll obviously be in a good position.”

Obviously, Nvidia seems to agree.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Dolly Parton’s Cousin Shares New Details on Her Health Battle Before Her Death
articles.excerpt: Dolly Parton’s first cousin Richie Owens has shared that the country music icon kept her health struggles private from even some family members.
articles.content:
Ariana Brockington

Trending News Reporter

Dolly Parton’s first cousin Richie Owens has shared that the country music icon kept her health struggles private from even some family members in the time leading up to her death, choosing instead to keep everyone optimistic.

The country music legend and actor died on Aug. 25 at the age of 80 from what a family spokesperson said was “a brief battle with cancer.”

Owens, who was a musical collaborator with Parton and also serves as the Parton family historian, stopped by TODAY Sept. 3 to speak about her life and legacy. Parton had shared in the months leading to her death that she had been struggling with health issues but did not publicly state that she had cancer.

“She of course posted herself that she had been going through health problems, but no one really knew what a lot of that was, including myself,” Owens said. “She always kept things private because she always wanted to keep everybody being positive around her and put that out there in the world. Just, ‘Don’t worry about me, I’m going to be fine.’ Just show the love.”

Owens also clarified reports that there was a formal funeral for his beloved cousin. Owens’ father, Louis, was the brother of Parton’s mother, Avie Lee Owens.

Parton was laid to rest alongside her husband of 59 years, Carl Dean, who died at 82 in 2025. Parton’s family confirmed that she was buried in Nashville on Aug. 28.

“She wanted to keep it very quiet,” Owens said. “The word keeps getting brought up, ‘funeral,’ and I don’t believe that was really the case in this situation. It was a burial, to be buried beside her husband.

“And she wanted it very small, and a few family members were there,” he added. “Other people that I’m sure would’ve liked to have been there were either out doing other things and stuff. It was very quiet, very quickly done, and not for any bad reasons whatsoever, it’s just that’s what she wanted. She wanted to keep it very, very private.”

Owens believes Parton, a noted philanthropist, would want any money spent mourning her loss to be spent on helping others.

“That’s exactly what she said ... when that happens to her, when she passes, she would much rather see people take that $50 you should spend on flowers and give it to her Imagination Library,” Owens said. “She’s said that many, many times. She really cared about her charities.”

The news of Parton’s death was first shared in a video message from her nephew Bryan Seaver posted on her Instagram account.

“This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago before I fully absorbed it as a future reality,” Seaver said, adding that fulfilling that request was “an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness.”

An obituary posted on her Facebook account read, “A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family.”

articles.title: IRS audit revenue plunged following workforce reductions, Treasury watchdog finds
articles.excerpt: IRS audits collected $3.5 billion less in fiscal 2025 as the agency shed thousands of auditors and other agency staffers.
articles.content:
Updated on: September 1, 2026 / 4:40 PM EDT / CBS News

Revenue from IRS audits plunged 35% in fiscal 2025 as the agency shed thousands of enforcement workers, according to a new report from the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration, an agency watchdog.

The IRS collected a total of $6.5 billion from audits in fiscal 2025, which ended Sept. 30, down from $10 billion a year earlier, TIGTA said in its Aug. 26 report.

The group said that the number of IRS employees working in auditing and collections had dropped to 17,517 as of January 2026, a decline of almost 10,000 workers from fiscal 2024. The report added that the impact of the staff reductions may "become more apparent over time." 

"These losses present a challenge to improving taxpayer service and enforcing the nation's tax laws," the tax watchdog said. "We are concerned about how staffing losses are impacting the IRS's ability to ensure that it meets department priorities."

Tax auditor exodus

The findings come after TIGTA last year found that the IRS lost one-third of its tax auditors during the first three months of the Trump administration. The employment decline was due to cost-cutting efforts by Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, which sought to slash the federal workforce through a combination of layoffs and so-called deferred resignations.

The Treasury watchdog noted that because audits can take years to complete, some of the declines could be reversed as more cases are closed. 

The IRS initiated 17% more large corporate audits in fiscal 2025 than a year earlier. But audits of new business partnerships fell 30% as a major reorganization at the agency shifted employees and delayed training for some revenue agents, the report said.

The IRS also started fewer audits of wealthy taxpayers. Agency staffers opened about 43,000 examinations of individuals with income over $400,000 in fiscal 2025, down 26% from a year earlier. As of January 2026, the agency's Global High Wealth program had 27% fewer employees than before the fiscal 2025 workforce reductions.

The Treasury didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. 

Rising tax receipts

The IRS pointed to comments made by its CEO, Frank Bisignano, during congressional testimony in April, in which he said the agency is increasingly relying on technology to improve enforcement. 

"Our advanced data and analytic strategies allow us to catch instances of tax evasion that would have been undetectable just a few years ago," Bisignano said. "Along those lines, the IRS is using artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced analytics to identify high-risk areas of non-compliance and fraud with greater accuracy."

Despite the decline in audit revenue, the IRS collected more total tax revenue in fiscal 2025 than the prior year, with federal taxes paid by taxpayers rising to $5.3 trillion, up 4.2% from the prior fiscal year, according to the Treasury watchdog group.

But Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts who has championed a federal wealth tax, said the data show that IRS employment cuts are a "dream come true" for high-income earners and corporations that skirt tax laws. 

"Gutting the IRS is a win for wealthy tax cheats and a loss for working people who play by the rules," she said in a statement to CBS News.

IRS funding cuts

The drop in audit revenue marks a reversal from 2024, when the IRS planned to boost tax revenue through audits of wealthy taxpayers and corporations. Under the Biden administration, the Inflation Reduction Act directed $80 billion in funding to the IRS, enabling it to hire more auditors and revenue collectors. 

In early 2024, the IRS forecast that the additional funding would help it reap hundreds of billions of dollars in additional tax revenue by pursuing overdue and unpaid taxes. However, Republican lawmakers warned that IRS auditors would target everyday Americans and cut billions in IRS funding. 

The Trump administration has proposed additional IRS funding cuts for 2027. Policy experts have warned that further shrinking the agency's budget could make it harder to collect overdue taxes and go after tax cheats. 

"The agency has fewer revenue agents, who audit the most complicated tax returns, than it has had since the 1950s, when the economy was far smaller and the tax code was far less complex," tax analysts with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan think tank, wrote in a June blog post. 

They added, "Research shows that every dollar spent on IRS tax enforcement raises multiple dollars in revenue, which means that every dollar cut from IRS enforcement loses more than a dollar of revenue and adds to the deficit."

articles.title: The IRS slashed its staff. One result? More taxes going uncollected
articles.excerpt: The IRS slashed its auditing staff last year — but the move may have backfired as tax collections from enforcement efforts plummeted, an Inspector General report shows.
articles.content:
Economy

The IRS slashed its staff. One result? More taxes going uncollected

  • Download
  • <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5954022/nx-s1-9911270" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">

A new Inspector General's report shows that as the IRS slashed its auditing ranks last year, collection of unpaid taxes fell. Karen Bleier/AFP hide caption

The IRS slashed its auditing staff last year in what was billed as a cost-cutting move, but if the effort was designed to improve the government's bottom line, it has backfired.

A new report from the Treasury Department's Inspector General for Tax Administration shows that revenue from audits plunged 35% in fiscal year 2025, meaning billions of dollars in taxes went un-collected. The drop coincides with a 27% cut in enforcement and collection staffing at the IRS, as part of Elon Musk's campaign to boost government efficiency.

"The downstream effects of these reductions are likely to become more apparent over time," the Inspector General wrote.

The IRS had beefed up its auditing ranks during the Biden administration, in an effort to collect more of the estimated $696 billion dollars in taxes that go unpaid every year, mostly as a result of people and businesses that under-report their income.

The increased staffing led to a 41% increase in audit-related revenue in 2024 — but that was largely reversed last year. More than 25,000 IRS employees were laid off or took early retirement in 2025, including about 3,600 tax examiners.

The loss in tax revenue from decreased audit activity outweighs any savings from reduced staffing at the tax-collection agency.

"Defunding the IRS is not a money-saving proposition because you have fewer employees," says Natasha Sarin, who served as a counselor on tax policy to former Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen. "It is a money-losing one, because you do a less good job of collecting taxes."

Audits generated $10 billion in tax revenue in fiscal year 2024 but that dropped to $6.5 billion in 2025.

Tax audits have been a tool to increase compliance

The Inspector General notes that the overall loss of revenue could be larger, since tax audits are primarily designed to promote voluntary tax compliance by filers wanting to avoid one.

"You're less likely to speed when you know that there's a cop on the beat," says Sarin, who's now a professor at Yale Law School.

IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank Bisignano defended the agency's tax enforcement record. Bisignano told lawmakers earlier this year the agency is using technology to target its tax audits more efficiently.

The increased staffing at the IRS under the Biden administration was aimed at bringing increased scrutiny to wealthy individuals and partnerships. That fell off sharply as thousands of auditors were let go. Audits of partnerships fell 76% between 2023 and 2025.

"Disproportionately, this is about the tip-top of the [income] distribution," Sarin says. "Something like the top 1% of earners are responsible for something like a third of the tax gap."

Staffing levels at the IRS continued to decline in the first four months of the current fiscal year. The Trump administration has called for additional cuts in agency funding in 2027.

New York Yankees @ Los Angeles Angels

ANAHEIM, Calif. -- — Cam Schlitter gave up one run and two hits in eight superb innings, and the New York Yankees scored five two-out runs in 10th in a 6-3 victory over the Los Angeles Angels on Wednesday night.

New York loaded the bases with one out in the 10th when Jose Caballero singled, the automatic runner holding at third, and Jazz Chisholm Jr. walked against reliever Luke Murphy (0-2).

Murphy got Luis Garcia Jr. to pop out, but Austin Wells stroked a two-run single to right, Cody Bellinger hit an RBI single to center, Trent Grisham hit an RBI single to left, and Ben Rice had an RBI single to right for a 6-1 lead.

David Bednar (7-3) struck out three in a scoreless ninth for the win. Yankees reliever Michael Fulmer gave up a two-run homer to Moisés Ballesteros in the bottom of the 10th.

A marquee matchup between two of baseball’s best pitchers did not disappoint, Schlittler striking out nine and walking none and Angels left-hander Reid Detmers allowing one run and six hits in seven innings, striking out eight and walking none.

Schlittler, who has an AL-best 2.04 ERA, retired 20 of the first 21 batters he faced, his only blemish a soft single to left by Vaughn Grissom in the second.

But he grooved a 95-mph cutter to Grissom in the seventh, and the Angels first baseman drove it over the center-field wall for a solo homer and a 1-1 tie.

It was Schlittler’s franchise-record 19th start in which he has allowed one or no runs, moving him ahead of Ron Guidry (1978), Whitey Ford (1964) and Jack Chesbro (1904), who had 18 each.

Detmers, who has a major league-best 1.52 ERA since the All-Star break, gave up a run in the fourth on Amed Rosario’s RBI double.

The game was delayed for about 10 minutes in the sixth when a 79.5-mph line drive off the bat of Rice hit a photographer in the head in the first-base camera well. The photographer was able to walk to a medical emergency vehicle and shake Rice’s hand before being carted away.

Six-time major winner Rory McIIlroy made admissions over his enthusiasm for competing at the highest level at the FedExCup; The Sky Sports Golf Podcast discussed McIlroy's future and what he may need to motivate him to get back to being world No 1

Rory McIlroy needs to assess how much he truly wants to be world No 1 again alongside balancing his home life, according to Sky Sports' Robert Lee.

The Northern Irishman finished in a seven-way tie for fourth at the FedExCup over the weekend, finishing five shots off tournament winner Scottie Scheffler despite showing earlier signs of promise.

Now 37, six-time major winner McIlroy admitted his "fuse was shorter than it used to be" before the final round at the East Lake Golf Club.

He had arrived in Atlanta off the back of three weeks of competing in a row, something he admitted he would never exceed again despite still managing a fourth-place finish over the weekend.

"That just tells you how good he is," Lee told the Sky Sports Golf Podcast. "But I think Rory's body language this week wasn't great. He looked slightly… is grumpy the right word?

"But he's just slightly off that kind of affable, bouncy Rory that we normally see. So there's stuff going on with him… Rory's in this position. He's played golf for 20 years at the highest level. He's 37.

"He realises there are other things in life, but the last thing he wants to do is not be able to be peak Rory. So his conundrum is 'how much can I pare back my schedule, but still perform the way I know I can?' That's the place he's in now.

"37 is still golfing prime. It's going to come down, for him, to desire. How much does he still want it? And if he still wants it, I think he's going to have to play a bit more."

McIlroy took an extended break after The Open, spending more time with his family before returning for this three-week run of events.

"I absolutely think he can win more majors," Lee continued. "But going along with that is you sacrifice your home life. You're not as home as much as you want to be… I actually think Rory is in mentally quite a good place at the moment, and he is focused on some family stuff at the moment."

Speaking before his final round, McIlroy admitted: "once you lose your enthusiasm to go to the course, it is time to take a break." That comment could suggest golf fans could be seeing less and less of the world No 2 as time goes on.

"I think that's plausible," Sean Zak, writer for Golf.com, agreed. "I think that the changes coming to the PGA Tour schedule could pull a little bit more out of him, could help him balance being a dual member a little bit better."

Zak went on to suggest McIlroy may need to set himself a goal of beating Scheffler to top spot to reignite his motivation.

"You know, of all the golfers at the top of the game, I think he better than most shows what things matter to him and shows the goals that he's set," he said.

"And I think ever since that Grand Slam-finishing Masters win, he has just struggled to really place "OK, what's the next goal?"

"When you look at 2025, when he won that Masters, the next goal was really, 'OK, let's win at Bethpage' - and then they did that.

"Then after that, it was 'gosh, OK, what is the next goal?' I think for him to live up to what we're asking him to do right now, what a lot of fans would like him to do, is his next goal needs to be taking Scottie off the top mark or matching Scottie in some way.

"I bet if Scottie won a major this year, Rory might feel a little bit more of the fire beneath him because you get to some point where they've all won a bunch.

"What is the tiebreaker? How many majors did you win? Rory still has a nice little lead on Scottie - but how long will that last? We think that he probably won't hold that lead.

"It's just funny because I think Rory McIlroy, let's say [at] 21 years old was like "I want to be number one in the world. I want to win every single tournament."

"Rory McIlroy, 37-year-old, he may have to do the same thing. It should be 'I want to be number one. I want the world to think I'm the best golfer because at my best, I certainly am.'"

What's next?

McIlroy will take a week off before returning to defend his Amgen Irish Open title, held at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg from September 10-13, a year on from his dramatic play-off win at The K Club.

The six-time major champion spoke candidly about his shrinking schedule after his third round at the Tour Championship

LIV Golf Collapse Is Here And The PGA Tour Has A BIG Problem | Don't @ Me w/ Dan Dakich

LIV golf is all but finished, but a dark cloud now hangs over the players: what happens next? Dan Dakich and crew discuss how the PGA will respond.

Golf is often seen as a very staid, traditional sport where little changes over time. But the past few years have been a tumultuous period in the professional game, at least, with the rise and now seeming fall of the LIV Golf Tour.

LIV's impact hasn't just been limited to their events, players and debate over how their tournaments should be weighed for major qualification or evaluated for Ryder Cup team selection. The PGA Tour, in response to LIV's formation, was essentially forced to make changes to keep top players in place.

Signature events with higher purses. Changing some tournaments to have no cuts. More support for the big names. All changed how the tour worked and who played in what events. The signature events enjoyed better competition as star players competed for $20 million in prize money, but some smaller tournaments suffered as golfers chose rest rather than travel and play for smaller rewards.

McIlroy committed to the PGA Tour when others were bolting, assumed a leadership role with commissioner Jay Monahan on the PGA's response and has become increasingly vocal as he becomes a "veteran" at 37-years-old.

And with the tour facing an even more aggressive set of changes under new CEO Brian Rolapp, McIlroy spoke about what that might mean for his schedule. Which seems to be decreasing each season.

After his third round at the Tour Championship in Atlanta, McIlroy admitted that his interest in playing most tournaments has decreased as he progresses through his career.

"This is my third week in a row. I rarely do that anymore, and I feel like that is my limit," he said.

"If I had to tee up again next week, that to me is tough."

He also said he'll never play four straight weeks in a row moving forward, and that his "fuse" has gotten shorter over time.

"But again, I am 37. This is my 18th or 19th year as a professional, so my fuse is a little shorter than it used to be," he added.

As for the reduced schedule he wants to play, McIlroy said it's likely going to get even smaller, "I play my schedule and I'll continue to play my schedule, which is getting less and less as the years go on."

Regarding the changes made to the PGA Tour moving forward, two different "tracks" for events, as well as promotion and relegation for the first time ever, he doesn't seem too excited for what that might mean. And blames LIV, in some small part, for what's happened.

articles.title: Sony and Microsoft seek dismissal of consumer lawsuits regarding tariff refunds
articles.excerpt: Sony and Microsoft have submitted motions to dismiss class action lawsuits alleging they failed to transfer tariff refunds to consumers.
articles.content:
Sony and Microsoft have submitted legal motions to have class action lawsuits against them dismissed. These lawsuits claim the companies did not return tariff refunds to consumers.

According to Game File, the suits came in response to price hikes in 2025 for the PlayStation 5 and Xbox consoles. Consumers allege these increases were driven by unlawful tariffs as determined by the US Supreme Court, who have since declared them illegal, suggesting customers are owed refunds.

Sony has asked a California Northern District judge to dismiss the case, asserting there's no legal obligation to pass tariff refunds to consumers.

The company's attorneys argued that the reasons behind the price hikes were not related to tariffs but rather to factors such as inflation, exchange rates, component costs, logistics, market competition, and consumer demand.

Furthermore, they highlighted that Sony has continued to raise hardware prices following the Supreme Court's decision on tariffs.

"Had tariffs been the reason for the original price increase, there would have been no justification for raising prices again post-tariff invalidation," stated Sony's legal team.

"If tariffs solely influenced price alterations, price reductions would be expected after their removal. Instead, the pricing strategy reflects various input costs."

In a July announcement, Sony projected a $508 million refund on tariffs, which resulted in a 37% increase in Q1 operating profits according to reports.

Microsoft mirrored Sony's rationale in a separate legal filing in Washington State Federal Court, seeking case dismissal as well.

"There is nothing unfair about a customer buying an Xbox at the stated price and receiving what they paid for, irrespective of later claims about Microsoft's pricing strategy," argued Microsoft.

Microsoft further stated the lawsuit lacked evidence supporting any price variation linked to tariffs, nor any feasible way to retrospectively compute tariff-related cost assessments.

Nintendo similarly sought dismissal of a class action lawsuit in July, highlighted in legal filings.

Nintendo's defense argued that consumers had the option to refrain from purchasing or to explore alternatives instead of accepting the listed prices. Nintendo emphasized that it did not uniformly apply tariff costs across all products but rather implemented targeted pricing changes, opting to absorb some tariff costs on popular products like the Switch 2.

To date, Panic, the Playdate producer, remains the sole hardware firm to return tariff surcharges following a refund from the government.

articles.title: Sony Says It Won't Pass Tariff Refunds Back to PlayStation Customers, and Dismisses Fan Arguments as 'Speculative and Illogical'
articles.excerpt: Sony has dismissed calls to return some of the $500 million it will receive in tariff refunds, despite having already passed its extra costs onto consumers through console price rises.
articles.content:
Says tariff-hiked PS5 sales were "voluntarily purchased."

Sony has dismissed calls from PS5 owners to return some of the $500 million it will receive in tariff refunds, despite having already passed its extra costs onto consumers through console price rises.

The PlayStation maker has said it expects to recoup around half a billion dollars from the U.S. government, with the majority of this amount flowing back into its gaming division.

Some PS5 owners say Sony should now return some of this windfall back to them, as the company has effectively now been paid twice — in the returned tariffs, and in the extra money it charged consumers following PS5 price rises, made during the era of tariffs to ensure it didn't lose its profit margins.

The 100 Best PlayStation Games of All Time

Sony is far from the only company in this position, with Nintendo and Microsoft previously being pushed by fans to do the same. (Panic, the maker of indie handheld Playdate, has said it will do so, however.)

Now, in a response to legal action attempting to force Sony to hand back some of the money, the PlayStation maker has made similar arguments to those companies, and said that its customers made their own decision to buy a PS5 console at the stated price. In other words: no one was forcing them to do so, and the consoles were sold at the price that was advertised.

"Paying fair market price for voluntarily purchased consumer goods is not a legally cognizable injury," Sony's lawyers argued in a legal motion reported by Game File.

In August, Microsoft's own lawyers stated similar: "There is nothing unjust about Plaintiff purchasing an Xbox at an advertised price and getting exactly what he paid for — regardless of whatever theory he devised months later about Microsoft's cost structure."

Now, Sony is also now pushing back on what it has described as the "speculative and illogical" argument that its PS5 price hikes around the time of the tariffs were specifically caused by the tariffs. Instead, Sony has attempted to argue, its price rises were the product of a larger combination of factors, such as "inflation, currency fluctuations, component costs, logistics, competitive dynamics, or demand."

Going even further, Sony has argued that its most recent PS5 price rise is actually evidence of this in practice, as it came after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the tariffs were illegal.

"If tariffs were the cause of the price increases, one would expect [PlayStation] to lower prices once the tariffs were eliminated — not raise them again. Instead, the timeline confirms that the pricing of PlayStation consoles includes a diverse and dynamic set of input costs."

In other words, Sony is saying that its decision to charge PS5 customers more money is proof that it needed to charge PS5 customers more money — an argument that will be interesting to see ruled on by a judge.

articles.title: 'No steering wheel, no pedals.' Tesla teases fans ahead of long-awaited Cybercab update
articles.excerpt: Tesla first unveiled the Cybercab almost two years ago, and fans of the company have been waiting to hear more.
articles.content:
In this article

Tesla's fledgling Robotaxi business teased fans with a post on X saying, "no steering wheel, no pedals," a reference to the company's forthcoming Cybercab driverless vehicles. Another post prompted riders to "try it out" in Austin, Texas, and CEO Elon Musk said in a pinned post, "A storm of Cybercabs."

Those comments on Wednesday came ahead of a planned event in Austin, where Tesla is expected to share more Cybercab details on Thursday. The company debuted the design of the vehicle almost two years ago.

Musk's automaker designed the Cybercab as a driverless two-seater with butterfly doors that it said will have no steering wheel or pedals. The company has been testing a version of the "purpose-built" robotaxi with human drivers and traditional controls in multiple markets across the U.S.

New Street Research analyst Pierre Ferragu and Tesla fans also shared video clips on X on Wednesday showing Cybercab vehicles circulating on public streets in Austin, with no steering wheel or driver on board.

Bullish investors are betting the company will soon unleash a torrent of robotaxis in a number of U.S. cities, as Tesla tries to eat into Waymo's big early lead.

Since at least 2016, Musk has told fans and investors that a Tesla vehicle capable of driving itself across the country without any human intervention was near. That still hasn't happened.

Tesla currently sells cars with a system called FSD — short for Full Self-Driving (Supervised). They require a human driver to remain at the wheel, ready to steer or brake at any time.

One Tesla Robotaxi tracker estimates that Tesla had just over 200 vehicles in its U.S. fleet that are registered as "unsupervised," capable of operating without a human driver on board, at least in geofenced areas of certain cities where they are allowed.

Tesla's "unsupervised" vehicles have logged trips in cities including Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando and Tampa, Florida, the tracker says.

Tesla also runs a chartered car service in the San Francisco area dubbed the FSD (Supervised) Rideshare service. The cars in that fleet are newer Model Y vehicles driven by Tesla employees, who use a version of the company's FSD (Supervised) which is not yet publicly available, according to Tesla terms of service. Passengers can hail the vehicles using the Tesla Robotaxi-branded app.

Meanwhile, Google's Waymo is operating a commercial robotaxi service in 14 U.S. cities, with a fleet of about 4,000 driverless vehicles on U.S. roads, and testing in additional markets.

In a note ahead of the expected Cybercab update, Morgan Stanley analysts said if the event "includes a meaningful rollout of unsupervised" vehicles, they expect Tesla's stock to "regain momentum." Tesla shares are down about 21% this year as of Wednesday's close.

However, if the event underwhelms, the analysts said, the market reaction would be muted or negative. Morgan Stanley has a $400 price target on Tesla and the equivalent of a hold rating.

"Continued growth in the unsupervised fleet (Cybercab or Model Y) is key for the stock to outperform through year-end," the analysts wrote.

Tesla had 45 Cybercab vehicles authorized for driverless operations in the state of Texas, out of a total 420 vehicles registered in the state, for driverless operations as of Wednesday night, according to public records on the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles website.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating Tesla in at least two ongoing probes concerning possible safety defects with its partially automated driving systems. Tesla has also been criticized for asking the NHTSA to redact far more information from its crash reports than other AV companies, effectively hiding safety data from public view.

articles.title: Boeing finds US$1.9 billion hole after bringing Spirit AeroSystems back in-house, report says
articles.excerpt: Unexpected costs from the US$8.4 billion acquisition are weighing on Boeing Commercial Airplanes as the manufacturer works to increase 737 MAX and 787 production
articles.content:
Boeing has found that the liabilities inherited with its acquisition of Spirit AeroSystems exceed identifiable assets by approximately US$1.9 billion, adding an unexpected financial burden as the US manufacturer works to accelerate production of the 737 MAX and 787.

The figure was calculated by The Wall Street Journal from Boeing's financial disclosures following the completion of the Spirit acquisition in December 2025. Boeing agreed to bring its former supplier back in-house primarily to gain greater control over manufacturing and quality, particularly on the 737 program.

The newspaper's analysis shows that the financial consequences have become considerably larger than initially apparent. Boeing valued the total consideration for Spirit at US$8.39 billion, including shares issued to Spirit stockholders, previous advances and debt assumed or repaid as part of the transaction.

Boeing's own second-quarter filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission provides further evidence of the costs it inherited.
